subject: mathematics
question_text: Prove by mathematical induction that a + (a + d) + (a + 2d) + … up to n terms = (n/2)[2a + (n − 1)d].

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IA (2026-27 edition), book p.26, chapter 4 MATHEMATICAL INDUCTION, Short Answer question 2. Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the Mathematics-IA volume prints no per-step mark allocation on any answer. The split gives one mark to each of the four moves an induction proof is marked on — the base case, the hypothesis, the inductive step and the closing appeal to the principle — and leaves the opening statement step unmarked, matching every other card in this chapter. Paper position: Maths-1A Section B prints eight short answers of which the student writes any six, each worth 4 marks, and Mathematical Induction supplies one of them on almost every paper. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove the A.P. sum by induction — what is held fixed, what the induction runs on, and what you add in the third step.

steps.label: Write the statement
steps.margin_note: Unmarked setup at 4 marks. Say clearly that a and d are fixed and the induction runs on n alone — that sentence is what makes the proof valid.
lines: Here a and d are fixed real numbers.
The induction is on n only.

recall.must_convey: That a and d stay fixed throughout and the induction runs on n only, and that the nth term is a + (n−1)d.
accept: a and d are fixed and the induction is only on n and the nth term is a plus n minus one d
hold the first term and the common difference fixed and induct on the number of terms
general term a plus n minus one times d then write out s of n
a and d fix chesi n meeda matrame induction cheyyali
heard_as: a plus n minus one d

steps.why: Two letters are floating in this question. Saying that a and d are fixed and that only n changes is what makes S(n) a statement about one variable, which is the only kind induction can prove.
common_mistakes: Writing the nth term as a + nd instead of a + (n−1)d.
Trying to induct on d or on a as well as on n.
steps.memory_tip: The nth term is a + (n−1)d: the first term has taken no steps yet, so n = 1 gives a.

steps.label: Check S(1)
steps.margin_note: One mark. At n = 1 the bracket (n−1)d becomes 0 — write that line out rather than skipping to a.
lines: ∴ L.H.S = R.H.S, so S(1) is true.

recall.must_convey: That at n = 1 the left side is a, and the right side is half of 2a plus zero times d, which is also a.
accept: left side is just a and right side is half of two a plus zero d which is a
put n equals one and the n minus one d term vanishes leaving a on both sides
the first case gives a on each side
n equals one pettina rendu sides a vasthai

steps.why: The single-term sum is just a. Showing the formula also gives a is the check that the (n−1) in the bracket is placed correctly.
common_mistakes: Asserting S(1) is true without working out both sides.
Putting n = 1 into (n−1)d and getting d instead of 0.
steps.memory_tip: At n = 1 the (n−1)d part is zero, so the right side is half of 2a, which is a.

steps.label: Assume S(k) is true
steps.margin_note: One mark. Assume it for ONE value k, with a and d unchanged, and number the line (1).
lines: Step 2 — assume S(k) is true, k ∈ N

recall.must_convey: That S(k) is assumed true for some k in N — the sum of k terms equals (k/2)[2a + (k−1)d], with a and d unchanged — and the line is numbered (1).
accept: assume the sum of k terms is k by two into two a plus k minus one d
suppose s of k holds with the same a and d and call it equation one
take it as true for one value k in the naturals and number the line
k ki true ani assume chesi equation one ga rastam
reject: let it be true for k
then I assume s of k

steps.why: Only n is replaced by k. Keeping a and d as the same letters is what allows the answer at k+1 to be compared with the formula.
common_mistakes: Assuming the statement for ALL k, which assumes what is being proved.
Changing a or d while replacing n by k.
steps.memory_tip: Replace n by k everywhere and leave a and d alone. Number the line (1).

steps.label: Show S(k+1) follows
steps.margin_note: One mark, and the longest step on the page. The next term is a + kd. Add it to both sides of (1) and collect the a terms and the d terms separately.
lines: Add it to both sides of (1):
So S(k+1) is true whenever S(k) is true.

recall.must_convey: That the next term a + kd is added to both sides of (1), the a terms give 2a(k+1) and the d terms give dk(k+1), so (k+1) comes out and the result is ((k+1)/2)(2a + kd).
accept: add a plus k d to both sides collect the a terms and the d terms and k plus one comes out of both
the a parts give two a into k plus one and the d parts give d k into k plus one
take k plus one over two out and what is left is two a plus k d
next term a plus k d add chesi k plus one common teestam
reject: I show s of k plus one
heard_as: two a into k plus one

steps.why: The d terms are k(k−1)d + 2kd, which is d(k² + k) = dk(k+1). That is where the shared factor (k+1) comes from, and it is the only step in the proof that needs care.
common_mistakes: Adding a + (k+1)d as the next term instead of a + kd.
Losing the 2 in the denominator when the next term is brought over.
Stopping at 2a + kd without writing it as the formula at k+1.
steps.memory_tip: The d terms are k(k−1)d + 2kd = d(k² + k) = dk(k+1). That is the shared (k+1).

steps.label: Conclude by P.M.I
steps.margin_note: The last mark is for naming the principle. One sentence, one full mark.
lines: Hence, by the principle of finite

recall.must_convey: That S(1) is true and S(k) implies S(k+1), so by the principle of mathematical induction the sum formula holds for every natural number n.
accept: since s of one is true and s of k gives s of k plus one by the principle of mathematical induction it holds for all n
hence by p m i the sum formula is true for every natural number
the base case and the inductive step together give it for all n in n
p m i prakaram anni natural numbers ki true

steps.why: The earlier steps prove two single statements — one about n = 1 and one about a step. Only the principle turns them into a claim about every n, for the fixed a and d.
common_mistakes: Writing only 'hence proved' and never naming the principle.
Claiming it for all real numbers instead of all n ∈ N.
steps.memory_tip: The closing sentence names the principle and is worth a full mark on its own.
